title: The Aachi of Chettinad: Meenakshi Meyyappan Keeps a Century-Old Cuisine Honest
excerpt: At 89, the matriarch of The Bangala in Karaikudi has spent two decades preserving Chettinad cooking as her family made it — temperate, subtle, and ground fresh on the ammi.
body:
• Meenakshi Meyyappan, the 89-year-old matriarch known as "aachi," turned the Meyyappan family mansion in Karaikudi into The Bangala — Chettinad's first heritage hotel — in 2000, training its chefs to cook the original recipes of her mother and mother-in-law.
  • She insists authentic Chettinad cooking is restrained, not fiery: no coconut in kootu, no cinnamon or cardamom in curries, and more coriander seed than chillies.
  • Her cookbook The Bangala Table documents 150 recipes from the region; the property also hosts the Chettinad Heritage & Cultural Festival.

The aachi who built a cuisine's archive

Meenakshi Meyyappan did not set out to become the custodian of Chettinad cuisine. When the family mansion in Karaikudi — "falling apart," she recalls — was nearly demolished, her son suggested restoring it as a heritage hotel instead. In 2000, at an age when most people retire, Meyyappan opened The Bangala, Chettinad's first heritage hotel, and built its kitchen around one rule: cook the way her mother and mother-in-law cooked.

"We trained our chefs to cook the original recipes of my mother-in-law and mother," says the 89-year-old, whom everyone calls aachi. Her co-authored cookbook, The Bangala Table: Flavors and Recipes from Chettinad, features 150 of those vegetarian and non-vegetarian recipes, and she is widely credited with preserving the region's cuisine in its purest form.

What Chettinad food really tastes like

Meyyappan's defining argument is restraint. Contrary to the cuisine's fiery reputation outside Tamil Nadu, she says Chettinad food is temperate and subtle. A typical kootu contains no coconut in any form — unlike much of the rest of Tamil Nadu — and is made with dal, no tempering, "only a little jeera and shallots." There is no room for cinnamon or cardamom in a typical curry: "We use more coriander seeds than chillies," she explains.

The repertoire includes getti kozhambu, thick curries unique to the region — brinjal and tamarind; paruppu urundai, crumbly balls of boiled dal soaked in a thick base; banana flowers first deep-fried as bajjis, then simmered in curry. In her younger years Meyyappan ate these kootus and kozhambus alongside mutton and chicken curries and offal soup — recipes with origins no one can trace, "passed down generation to generation." Precision is non-negotiable: "The vegetables must be cut finely, the masala ground in an 'ammi'. Food has to taste fine, it cannot be coarse in any way."

Keeping the lineage alive

The knowledge lives in people. Karuppaiya, a chef who spent 58 years at The Bangala, still visits from his village 15 kilometres from Karaikudi and makes the dangar — a thick curry of shallots and tamarind — whenever he comes. "It is people such as him who carry forward the recipes and cooking techniques handed down by Meyyappan's ancestors," The Hindu wrote of the household's kitchen culture.

Meyyappan herself keeps her distance from modern food fame. She is not on social media and prefers life at her own pace, hosting visitors from across cultures at the property. She created the Chettinad Heritage & Cultural Festival to give guests a taste of the region's traditions, customs and food; its second edition concluded in October.

A recipe from The Bangala Table: Mutton uppu kari

A dry-cooked mutton dish that shows Chettinad's signature logic — a small round chilli, gundu milagai, doing the work of a whole spice box. For 500g boneless mutton (in one-inch cubes, with a little liver for flavor): temper 25 seeded gundu milagai, a 1.5-inch cinnamon stick, 11 cloves garlic sliced lengthwise, 100g shallots, half a cup of chopped red onions and half a teaspoon of turmeric in 100ml hot oil. Add three-quarters cup sliced tomatoes and cook 3 minutes; add mutton and a teaspoon of salt, stir 4 minutes, then add a cup of water and simmer 30–45 minutes until fork-tender. Uncover and sauté until the water evaporates and the mutton is coated in sauce. Serve with rice.

nri_angle: For Tamil diaspora families whose Chettinad recipes have been simplified in migration, The Bangala Table and the festival offer a living reference for the cuisine's original restraint and technique.
